<ui-body id="intro" text="Water is never used up. It is constantly recycled between the surface and the atmosphere. This lesson covers the three main stages of the cycle, works through a calculation, and ends with a short self-check." />

<ui-heading id="concepts-heading" text="Three Core Concepts" />

<ui-concept_rung id="concept-evaporation" badge="1" kind="depth" title="Evaporation" body="The Sun heats water in oceans, lakes, and rivers. Liquid water gains enough energy to become water vapour, an invisible gas that rises into the air.

Plants add to this through transpiration, releasing vapour from their leaves. Together the two processes are called evapotranspiration." takeaway="Heat energy turns liquid water into vapour." />

<ui-concept_rung id="concept-condensation" badge="2" kind="depth" title="Condensation" body="As water vapour rises, the air cools. Cool air holds less vapour, so the vapour turns back into tiny liquid droplets around dust and salt particles.

Billions of these droplets gather to form clouds. The same process puts dew on grass and fog near the ground." takeaway="Cooling turns vapour back into liquid droplets." />

<ui-concept_rung id="concept-precipitation" badge="3" kind="depth" title="Precipitation and Collection" body="When cloud droplets merge and grow too heavy to stay airborne, they fall as rain, snow, sleet, or hail.

The water then collects in oceans, lakes, and rivers, soaks into the ground as groundwater, or runs off across the surface. From there the cycle starts again." takeaway="Gravity returns water to the surface, and the cycle restarts." />

<ui-callout id="cycle-callout" kind="tip" title="Remember the order" text="Evaporation, then condensation, then precipitation, then collection. The cycle has no true start or end." />

<ui-heading id="example-heading" text="Worked Example" />

<ui-concept_rung id="worked-example" badge="EX" kind="example" title="How much energy does it take to dry a puddle?" body="A puddle covers 1 m² and is 5 mm deep. Find the mass of water, then the heat energy the Sun must supply to evaporate it. Use a latent heat of vaporisation of about 2.26 MJ per kg." code="Volume = 1 m² × 0.005 m = 0.005 m³
Mass   = 0.005 m³ × 1000 kg/m³ = 5 kg
Energy = 5 kg × 2.26 MJ/kg = 11.3 MJ" code_caption="Evaporating one small puddle takes about 11 megajoules of solar energy." takeaway="Evaporation moves a huge amount of energy as well as water." />
